executive_assessment.text: Anseba's Habero/Hamelmalo water and agriculture evaluation adds concrete capacity and maintenance limits; older rainfall and solar-asset scenarios remain distinct.
Goluj illustrates historical war-related disruption of seasonal livestock water access, with localized resource tensions. This is not a current national climate-conflict trend.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2026-01-28 reports: At five consulted project sites, dams, diversions and water-harvesting structures still supported irrigation, pastoralism and hygiene; siltation and maintenance problems limited sustainability.

Source dated 2026-01-28 reports: Ministry-led MIHAP replication sustained agricultural diversification and livestock production; Anseba authorities reported 58 of 640 participating households became small or medium commercial enterprises.
The ex-post evaluation observed three of six hydromet stations: all three generated data, but two had partial functionality. Data were not centrally automated and farm advice was uneven.

Source dated 2026-01-28 reports: The evaluation found women’s participation and leadership sustained after the project; women reported reduced water-fetching burdens, and children’s school attendance improved.

Source dated 2002 reports: After the border war disrupted transhumance and Tekezze-Setit basin watering access, herds shifted to wells around Goluj and nearby return sites; the study reports emerging farmer–livestock-owner conflict.

Source dated 2002 reports: Rapid borehole development in Gash-Barka changed water use and encouraged larger livestock populations; the study cautioned that resource pressure could threaten poor returnee and stayee livelihoods.

Source dated 2002 reports: Around Goluj, respondents linked scarcer fuelwood to population-related forest depletion; poor households lacking transport or money reduced use, while animal owners could access markets.

Source dated 2012-11 reports: UNDP’s case study reports erratic below-average rain in 2002–2004, especially in parts of Habero, caused livestock losses and impaired livelihoods; annual rain ranged from 190 mm in Habero to about 367 mm in Hamelmalo.

Source dated 2012-11 reports: Anseba herders moved west in July–September and toward the eastern escarpment or Northern Red Sea in November–March; land-use pressure, degradation and settlement policies disrupted this practice.

Source dated 2024-03 reports: For solar-asset planning, GCA describes lowland and coastal rainfall below 100 mm with dry spells over 200 days, versus wetter highlands; drought hazard is very high across most Eritrea and dust/wind risk is elevated in Anseba.

known_gaps.text: The only opened explicit climate-conflict statement is a project proposal with an undated receipt field; no recent empirical conflict-impact assessment was opened.

National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.

No inspected current source establishes climate-caused armed conflict in Eritrea or current insecurity blocking adaptation. The ODI conflict and displacement findings are historical; the baseline project proposal describes water/resource conflict only as a prospective risk.
The AF-TERG evaluation visited eight of 16 project sites and is not a national or district-wide vulnerability survey.
AfDB’s 2025 WASH adaptation document listing returned HTTP 402, so its regional ESIAs and stakeholder plan could not be checked.
The GCA hazard chapter concerns solar and power assets and uses high-level climate modelling; it does not measure household or livelihood exposure.
Main directly checked the ex-post methods/hydromet findings and ODI Goluj passages. The reverse link concerns lost seasonal watering/mobility options, not a claim that climate caused the war.
AF-TERG's 2025 fieldwork visited selected sites and reports perceived/observed sustainability; GCA's solar-asset hazards are not household-loss estimates.
